name: Tom Steyer
role: Billionaire investor and climate activist; 2020 Democratic presidential candidate; 2026 California governor candidate
summary: Tom Steyer is a billionaire investor who made climate change his main cause and ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination on a platform of climate action, a wealth tax, term limits and a national referendum process. He ran for California governor in 2026, campaigning on taxing the wealthy, abolishing ICE and free public education, and he has moved to support single-payer health care.

universal-healthcare.rationale: In December 2025 he said 'Bernie Sanders was right. We need single-payer health care.' In 2019-2020 he opposed Medicare for All and backed an opt-in public option instead; the later statement is used as his most recent clear position.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In February 2020 he vowed to call for a $22 federal hourly minimum wage, reported in a news account of his campaign event.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Proposed a 1% annual tax on net worth above $32 million (October 2019) and, in 2026, said 'I'm the billionaire who wants to tax other billionaires' while supporting a one-time billionaire tax.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Campaign plans call for breaking 'the stranglehold that corporations exercise over our government' and for reforms on corporate money and lobbying; this points toward tighter regulation of corporate influence, though not a general regulatory agenda he stated.

limit-guns.rationale: His October 2019 gun plan proposed a national license for all gun ownership, a national registry for existing assault weapons and a ban on new ones. It does not extend to all guns.

abortion-legal.rationale: In 2017 at Netroots Nation he said 'We're pro-choice' and that his group would not work for any candidate who is not pro-choice, as reported by Politico. The remarks are about his political group's stance rather than a direct personal statement on abortion law.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Campaign platform: 'Declaring the climate crisis a national emergency on day one' and net-zero warming pollution by 2045; he called climate 'priority one'.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Called Trump's trade war 'a failure, hurting working Americans, hurting businesses, killing farmers' (October 2019). This opposes tariffs as used in that trade war, not tariffs in general.

direct-votes.rationale: His July 2019 plan called for an annual national referendum process on major issues, letting voters decide directly rather than through Congress.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Campaign platform called to 'eliminate our dependence on fossil fuels', end American fossil fuel exports and prevent drilling in the Arctic. Expansion of domestic production is not addressed directly.

death-penalty.rationale: Publicly supported Proposition 62 in 2016, the ballot measure to end capital punishment in California, via a press release.

ban-cartels.rationale: Pledged to 'break up utility monopolies' to lower electricity rates (2026). This is limited to utilities rather than cartels in general.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Told the AP in 2026 that anyone unwilling to pay 'your fair share' is 'spitting on those people'. This is a general statement about the duty of the wealthy to contribute to the public, not about looking after the less fortunate.

corporate-influence.rationale: Said the plan would 'break the stranglehold that corporations exercise over our government with their money and lobbying power' (October 2019), and that corporations are not people.

term-limits.rationale: Proposed 12-year term limits for members of Congress and the Senate, plus congressional term limits in his 2019 political reform plan.

free-public-college.rationale: Campaign issue headline in 2026: 'Provide Free Education From Pre-K to College'. The 2020 platform also called for pre-K through college education as a basic right.

notes: Health care changed over time: he opposed Medicare for All and backed a public option in 2019-2020, then in December 2025 said 'We need single-payer health care' and used the most recent statement. Most of the known answers come from his 2019-2020 campaign releases (American Presidency Project copies) and his 2026 issue page and reported remarks. Many statements are left null: the reviewed sources did not address them. Searches on unions, drug policy, Israel/Iran beyond the 2020 statement, and abortion beyond 2017 found too little usable text. Attempts to fetch the 2026 Substack ICE post and the Davis Vanguard interview failed (403) and the Bloomberg Law article was paywalled, so those are reported only through secondary coverage and Wikipedia. Two campaign-era items (the 2020 criminal justice plan and the 2019 marijuana interview) were found only in pages that could not be fetched, so they are not used.
